greek_itylus.name: Become the grief-song of the nightingale through a mother's lament
greek_itylus.notes: His accidental killing by his mother Aedon, who mistook him in the dark for the eldest son of Niobe, is the Homeric aetion of the nightingale's mournful spring song; Zeus turned the grieving Aedon into the bird whose endless trilling laments 'dear Itylus'.

sources.reference: Homer, Odyssey 19.518-523

greek_laertes.name: Sail among the Argonauts in his youth
greek_laertes.notes: Numbered among the Argonauts in the mythographic crew-rosters before he retired in age to his Ithacan farm.

sources.reference: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.86; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.9.16

greek_laertes.name: Be restored to martial vigour by Athena to fight in old age
greek_laertes.notes: In the closing battle of the Odyssey, Athena breathes strength into the aged Laertes so that he casts his spear and kills Eupeithes, father of Antinous.

sources.reference: Homer, Odyssey 24.516-525

greek_oenomaus.name: Overtake and slay daughter's suitors in the deadly chariot-race
greek_oenomaus.notes: Offered Hippodamia only to a suitor who could outrace him; with the swift horses given by Ares he overtook each contestant from behind and speared him, fixing the heads of the slain over his palace doors, until Pelops won by Myrtilus's sabotage of the lynchpins.

sources.reference: Pindar, Olympian 1.67-88; Apollodorus, Epitome 2.4-9

greek_pelias.name: Dispatch a rival on the deadly Argonautic quest
greek_pelias.notes: Warned by an oracle against a one-sandalled man, Pelias sent his nephew Jason to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis in the expectation that the voyage would destroy him.

sources.reference: Pindar, Pythian 4; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 1.9.16

greek_neoptolemus.name: Take Troy from within the Wooden Horse
greek_neoptolemus.notes: Fetched from Scyros by Odysseus because Troy could not fall without him, he was among the warriors hidden in the Wooden Horse and led the slaughter at the city's fall.

sources.reference: Homer, Odyssey 11.506-537; Apollodorus, Epitome 5.10-11

greek_neoptolemus.name: Cut down King Priam at the household altar
greek_neoptolemus.notes: At the sack he killed the aged Priam at the altar of Zeus Herkeios and flung the infant Astyanax from the walls, the defining acts of his ruthlessness.

sources.reference: Virgil, Aeneid 2.526-558; Apollodorus, Epitome 5.21-23

greek_laomedon.name: Cheat his hired wages from gods and heroes alike
greek_laomedon.notes: The proverbial perjurer: he withheld the wage promised to Apollo and Poseidon for building Troy's walls, then defrauded Heracles of the immortal horses owed for slaying the sea-monster and rescuing Hesione, bringing destruction on himself and his house.

sources.reference: Homer, Iliad 21.441-457; Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.9

greek_penelope.name: Hold off the suitors with the unfinished shroud
greek_penelope.notes: For three years she wove a funeral shroud for Laertes by day and unravelled it by night, deferring her promised choice of a suitor until a maid betrayed the trick.

greek_penelope.name: Test and recognize her returned husband by the secret of the marriage-bed
greek_penelope.notes: She proved the disguised stranger truly Odysseus by ordering the immovable bed moved, whose secret, that it was carved from a living olive rooted in the house, only he could know.

sources.reference: Homer, Odyssey 23.173-204

greek_phaedra.name: Destroy her stepson with a dying false accusation
greek_phaedra.notes: Seized by an Aphrodite-sent passion for her stepson Hippolytus and rejected by him, she hanged herself leaving a tablet that falsely accused him of rape, drawing down Theseus's curse and the bull from the sea that killed Hippolytus.

sources.reference: Euripides, Hippolytus 856-898
Pindar, Olympian 1.76-88 (he speared each suitor from behind)

greek_menelaus.name: Hero-cult of Menelaus at the Menelaion, Therapne
greek_menelaus.notes: Menelaus was worshipped jointly with Helen at the Menelaion, the heroon on the ridge of Therapne above Sparta; votive dedications inscribed to Helen and Menelaus from the seventh and sixth centuries BCE are among the earliest epigraphic evidence for the cult of any Homeric hero.

sources.reference: Herodotus 6.61; Pausanias 3.19.9; archaeological dedications from the Menelaion

greek_pelops.name: Chthonic hero-cult at the Pelopion, Olympia
greek_pelops.notes: Honoured above all heroes at Olympia in his precinct in the Altis: the Eleans sacrificed to him annually a black ram by night as to a chthonic power, the blood-offering preceding the daytime sacrifice to Zeus; the ephebes scourged themselves at his tomb, and his sanctuary was said to have been founded by Heracles.

sources.reference: Pindar, Olympian 1.90-93; Pausanias 5.13.1-3

greek_orestes.name: Hero-cult and transfer of the bones of Orestes to Sparta
greek_orestes.notes: On the bidding of the Delphic oracle the Spartans recovered the giant bones of Orestes from Tegea and reburied them at Sparta, gaining the upper hand over Tegea; thereafter Orestes was venerated as a protecting hero, his grave shown in the Spartan agora.

sources.reference: Herodotus 1.67-68; Pausanias 3.11.10

greek_neoptolemus.name: Hero-shrine and annual offerings at Delphi
greek_neoptolemus.notes: Slain at the Delphic altar and buried within the sanctuary, Neoptolemus received hero-cult from the Delphians, who offered him yearly sacrifice; his tomb beside the temple of Apollo was a recognised heroon.

sources.reference: Pindar, Nemean 7.44-47; Pausanias 10.24.6

greek_nicostratus.name: Lacedaemonian hero-cult of Nicostratus
greek_nicostratus.notes: Worshipped at Sparta alongside Aethiolas as a son of Menelaus and Helen, with active local hero-cult recorded by the scholiast on Iliad 3.175.

sources.reference: Scholia on Homer, Iliad 3.175; cf. Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.11.1

greek_olympias.name: Bacchic-Orphic serpent rites of the Macedonian Klodones and Mimallones
greek_olympias.notes: Plutarch records that Olympias led the orgiastic Dionysiac rites more zealously than other Macedonian women, the celebrants called Klodones and Mimallones; she introduced great tame serpents into the revels, which reared from the ivy and mystic baskets and coiled about the wands, terrifying the men.

sources.reference: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 2.5-9

greek_otrera.name: Foundation of the sanctuary of Artemis at Ephesus
greek_otrera.notes: The Amazon queen Otrera was credited with founding the Artemision, the great temple of Artemis at Ephesus, anchoring the Anatolian Greek cult of Artemis to the Amazon foundation-tradition.

sources.reference: Hyginus, Fabulae 223 (Otrera founder of the temple of Diana at Ephesus); cf. Pausanias 7.2.7

greek_linus.name: Argive festival of the Arnis and the dirge of Linus
greek_linus.notes: At Argos, after the child Linus (son of Apollo and Psamathe) was torn by dogs and avenged by the plague-spirit Poine, a festival of mourning was kept in which stray dogs were killed and lamentation was made for Linus and Psamathe with the dirge-cry ailinon.

sources.reference: Pausanias 1.43.7; Conon, Narrations 19

greek_panacea.name: Invocation among the Asclepiad healing deities
greek_panacea.notes: Named in the opening invocation of the Hippocratic Oath beside Apollo, Asclepius, and Hygieia, and worshipped with the family of Asclepius in the Asclepieia as a personification of universal cure.

sources.reference: Hippocratic Oath, opening lines

attributes.name: Conical sailor's cap (pilos)
attributes.notes: From the fifth century BCE Odysseus is regularly identified in art by the pilos, the pointed conical felt cap of seafarers and workmen, worn with a short beard and traveller's dress.

sources.reference: Attic vase-painting from the 5th c. BCE onward; LIMC s.v. Odysseus

attributes.name: Sword dropped at the sight of Helen's breast
attributes.notes: A favourite vase-painting type shows Menelaus advancing on Helen at the sack of Troy with drawn sword, then letting it fall, disarmed by her beauty, the visual counterpart of the reconciliation tradition.

sources.reference: Attic red-figure 'Recovery of Helen' scenes 5th c. BCE; LIMC s.v. Menelaos

attributes.name: Leda embraced by the swan
attributes.notes: The dominant image: the Spartan queen with the swan-Zeus in her arms or at her lap, a sculptural and painted type repeated throughout antiquity.

sources.reference: Hellenistic 'Leda and the Swan' sculptural type; Apollodorus 3.10.7

attributes.name: The egg of Leda on the altar
attributes.notes: In South-Italian and Attic vase-painting the egg from which Helen hatches stands on an altar between Leda and Tyndareus, with the Dioscuri attending.

sources.reference: Apulian and Attic red-figure egg-birth scenes 5th-4th c. BCE
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.10.7 (Zeus as a swan); Euripides, Helen 17-21

attributes.name: Rising from the earth, adorned by the gods
attributes.notes: In Attic vase-painting Pandora appears either as a stiff statue-like figure crowned and decked by the surrounding Olympians, or rising up out of the ground (an anodos type), often with Hephaestus and Athena at hand.

sources.reference: Attic red-figure 5th c. BCE (e.g. the Niobid Painter krater); Hesiod, Theogony 571-584

attributes.name: The pithos (storage-jar) of evils
attributes.notes: Her defining attribute is the great pithos which, opened, loosed the evils upon mankind and held back only Hope.

sources.reference: Hesiod, Works and Days 90-105

attributes.name: Lion-headed mask of Fear on the warrior's shield
attributes.notes: Phobos was figured as a face of terror, given a lion's head, set at the centre of Agamemnon's shield-boss and emblazoned on the Shield of Heracles, where he glares with fire-bright eyes amid the war-host.

sources.reference: Homer, Iliad 11.36-37; Hesiod, Shield of Heracles 144-160

attributes.name: Giant hunter with club, lion-skin, belt and sword
attributes.notes: Orion is identified by the hunter's club and lion-skin and, as the constellation, by his bright belt and the sword hanging from it; in the underworld Homer shows him still driving game with his unbreakable bronze club.

sources.reference: Homer, Odyssey 11.572-575 (Orion with his bronze club in Hades)

attributes.name: Bearded sea-elder, fish-tailed, in a chiton with staff or trident
attributes.notes: Attic vase-painters showed the draped, bearded torso of Nereus issuing from a long coiling scaly fish-tail; unlike Triton he is regularly clothed in a chiton and bears a staff of authority, sometimes a trident.

sources.reference: Attic black- and red-figure vase-painting; LIMC s.v. Nereus

attributes.name: Chariot-race against Oenomaus
attributes.notes: The east pediment of the Temple of Zeus at Olympia placed Pelops and Oenomaus before Zeus on the eve of the fatal race, the founding image of the Olympic site; the race was also shown on the Chest of Cypselus.

sources.reference: Pausanias 5.10.6-8 (east pediment); 5.17.7 (Chest of Cypselus)

attributes.name: The ivory shoulder
attributes.notes: His restored ivory shoulder, replacing the part eaten by Demeter when Tantalus served him to the gods, was a marvel shown to pilgrims and a token of his Pelopid descendants.

sources.reference: Pindar, Olympian 1.25-27; Pausanias 5.13.4-6

attributes.name: The dying queen, helmet pushed back, in the leopard-skin
attributes.notes: Exekias's amphora fixes the iconic moment: Achilles, masked by his helmet, drives his spear into the throat of Penthesilea, whose helmet is thrust back to bare her face in the instant their eyes meet; she wears the short chiton, leopard-skin, sword and shield of the Amazon.

sources.reference: Exekias, Attic black-figure amphora, British Museum (c. 530 BCE)

attributes.name: Seated mourning figure at the loom
attributes.notes: Penelope is recognised by her pensive seated pose, veiled, head bowed on one hand and legs crossed, often before the upright loom of the shroud, the visual emblem of faithful waiting.

sources.reference: Attic red-figure skyphos of the Penelope Painter (Chiusi, c. 440 BCE)

attributes.name: Phrygian shepherd judging the three goddesses
attributes.notes: Paris is shown as a youthful herdsman in Phrygian cap, holding the golden apple or the shepherd's staff, seated among his flocks as Hermes leads Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite before him for the Judgment.

sources.reference: Judgment of Paris in vase-painting from the 6th c. BCE; Apollodorus, Epitome 3.2

attributes.name: Duel with Achilles beneath the scales of Zeus
attributes.notes: The combat of Memnon and Achilles, often flanked by their mothers Eos and Thetis pleading with Zeus as he weighs their fates (the kerostasia), was a favourite of archaic and classical vase-painters.

sources.reference: Aethiopis (Arctinus); Attic vase-painting of the Achilles-Memnon duel
Pausanias 10.31.6; Ovid, Metamorphoses 13.576-622 (the birds born of his pyre that fight and lament yearly at his tomb)

attributes.name: Singer enthroned amid charmed beasts and Thracians
attributes.notes: Orpheus is figured seated with the lyre or kithara, his music drawing wild animals, birds, and listening Thracian warriors about him; the scene of the spell-bound creatures is among the most reproduced of all his images.

sources.reference: Attic vase-painting and later mosaics 'Orpheus among the animals'; cf. Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 1.26-31

attributes.name: Bearded king enthroned as judge of the dead
attributes.notes: On Cretan coins Minos appears bearded and diademed as the royal lawgiver; in underworld scenes on vases and Roman sarcophagi he sits enthroned among the dead with Aeacus and Rhadamanthys, sometimes with the staff or sceptre of judgement.

sources.reference: Homer, Odyssey 11.568-571 (Minos giving judgement among the dead); Cretan coinage

sacredAnimals.name: Bull (of the Cretan thalassocracy and the Minotaur)

sources.reference: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 3.1.3-4 (the Cretan bull and the birth of the Minotaur)
